hints: Look at the atoms inside each dashed box in Fig. 1.1. Which box contains only N and H, and which box contains C, O and OH?
Recall the two functional groups found in every amino acid - one is basic and contains nitrogen, the other is acidic and contains C=O and OH.
walkthrough:
Recall the General Amino Acid Structure**
Every amino acid has a central carbon joined to an amine end and an acid end. The left box shows $H-N-H$, which is nitrogen-containing and basic. The right box shows $C=O$ with $OH$, which is carbon-containing and acidic.

Name A and B Correctly**
A is the amino group ($-NH_2$). B is the carboxyl group ($-COOH$). These are the two groups that will later react to form a peptide bond.
Final answer: A = amino (amine) group; B = carboxyl group.

hints: Think about which two groups must meet - the acid end of one glycine and the amine end of the other. Which side should face which?
Remember condensation removes the atoms that make water. Which $OH$ and which $H$ are lost from the two groups?
After water is lost, what new link is left between C and N, and what must still be shown correctly on either side as $C=O$ and $N-H$?
walkthrough:
Set Up a Condensation**
Proteins form by condensation. The $OH$ from the carboxyl group ($-COOH$) of the left glycine and one $H$ from the amino group ($-NH_2$) of the right glycine are removed to make $H_2O$.

Draw the New Peptide Bond**
Join the carbon of the first $C=O$ directly to the nitrogen of the second amino group to make $C-N$. This is the peptide bond. You should now have: $H_2N-CH_2-C(=O)-NH-CH_2-COOH$.

Check the Details**
Keep the $C=O$ double bond on the left residue and a single $N-H$ on the link ($-CO-NH-$). Also show the water molecule formed as a product. This shows one dipeptide of glycine-glycine.
Final answer: Join $C$ of carboxyl of one glycine to $N$ of amine of the other by a peptide bond ($-CO-NH-$) with $C=O$ and $N-H$ shown correctly; $H_2O$ released by condensation.

hints: Antibodies are proteins, so their polypeptides are coded by genes made of DNA. Which large dark organelle in the centre of Fig. 1.3 stores DNA?
walkthrough:
Link Genes to Structure**
Genes are sections of DNA that code for polypeptides. In an animal cell DNA is held in the nucleus as chromatin. In Fig. 1.3 the large dark central body is the nucleus, so label T must point anywhere inside it.
Final answer: Label T with line to the nucleus (dark central region containing chromatin/DNA).

hints: Start with the magnification triangle: magnification = image size divided by actual size. Rearrange it to find actual size.
Measure line P-Q in mm on the paper, convert to $\mu$m by multiplying by 1000, then divide by 6000 and round to the nearest $\mu$m.
walkthrough:
Write the Governing Formula**
Use $magnification = \frac{image\ length}{actual\ length}$, so $actual\ length = \frac{image\ length}{magnification}$.

Substitute and Convert Units**
Measure P-Q. On the printed paper this is about $90\ mm = 90,000\ \mu m$ (since $1\ mm = 1000\ \mu m$). Then $actual = \frac{90,000}{6000} = 15\ \mu m$ to the nearest micrometre. Your measured mm may vary slightly, so accept $14-16\ \mu m$ if working is shown.
Final answer: actual diameter = image length / magnification; $\approx 15 \mu m$.

hints: A TEM image is an extremely thin slice through a 3D cell. If an organelle is not in that exact plane, will it appear?
walkthrough:
Think in 3D**
A plasma cell does contain many mitochondria to supply ATP for antibody synthesis, but a TEM section is only about 70-90 nm thick. Any mitochondria lying above or below that plane will not be visible, so few appear in this one slice.
Final answer: The micrograph shows only a very thin section through the cell; mitochondria present in other planes of the cell are not cut through in this section.

hints: Sieve tubes carry sugary sap by pressure-driven mass flow through sieve plates. How would bulky organelles in the lumen affect that flow?
If the sieve element has lost most organelles and cannot power itself, which neighbouring cell keeps it alive metabolically?
walkthrough:
Clear Lumen for Unblocked Flow**
Sieve tube elements transport sucrose solution by mass flow from source to sink. Having no nucleus, vacuole or many mitochondria leaves a wide, empty lumen. This reduces friction and resistance and allows a larger volume of sap to pass per unit time.

No Energy Need Inside the Tube**
Mass flow is driven by hydrostatic pressure gradients set up by loading and unloading, not by ATP made inside the sieve element. Any metabolic support needed is provided by the adjacent companion cell, which retains mitochondria and carries out living functions for both cells.

Final answer: Any two from: fewer organelles reduces resistance to flow of sap; leaves larger lumen so greater volume of sap flows per unit time; mass flow needs no ATP from sieve element itself; companion cell carries out metabolism for the sieve element.
